title: The Quiet Confession
premise: Kestrel Oyelaran, an insurance investigator whose photographic memory has never failed them, is hired by a nervous stranger who pays triple to prove that a murder in the coastal town of Marrow Bay hasn't happened yet — the victim is still alive, and someone intends to kill him before his retrial. As Kestrel digs, they discover the original conviction hinged on testimony they themselves gave years ago as a child witness, testimony their memory now tells them was wrong. Racing the trial date, Kestrel must expose the real killer — the town's beloved retired detective who orchestrated the first conviction — while confronting that belonging to Marrow Bay always required staying silent. The case closes not in a courtroom but in a confession Kestrel forces into the open, trading their own invisibility for justice.
about_author: Quentin Kavanagh is the pen name of a former claims adjuster who spent eleven years reconstructing other people's worst days from paperwork. They write mysteries about memory, complicity, and the small towns that keep their secrets like savings accounts.

chapters.title: Paid in Full
chapters.summary: Kestrel's POV. A client named Ada Voss hires Kestrel for an impossible job: prove that Daniel Okafor's murder hasn't happened yet, though everyone in Marrow Bay believes he died six years ago. The retainer is suspiciously generous. Beat: unease disguised as professional curiosity.

chapters.title: The Man Who Isn't Dead
chapters.summary: Kestrel's POV. Kestrel confirms Okafor is alive, hidden under a new name two towns over, awaiting retrial after his conviction was overturned on procedural grounds. Someone wants him dead before he can testify again. Beat: the case snaps into focus — prevention, not investigation.

chapters.title: Marrow Bay Remembers Differently
chapters.summary: Kestrel's POV. Returning to Marrow Bay, Kestrel finds a town united in grief for a murder that never occurred, complete with a memorial bench. Old neighbors greet them warmly — too warmly. Beat: belonging offered like a trap.

chapters.title: Photographs of Nothing
chapters.summary: Kestrel's POV. Kestrel's perfect recall begins replaying fragments of the night of the original crime: rain, a porch light, a voice they've never been able to place. Their memory, their pride, starts contradicting their sworn childhood statement. Beat: the ground tilts.

chapters.title: The Detective's Long Shadow
chapters.summary: Ada's POV. Ada reveals she's Okafor's sister and suspects retired Detective Chief Inspector Hollis Brand, the man who built the case and the town's gratitude around it. She has no proof, only patterns. Beat: grief sharpened into purpose.

chapters.title: Six Years of Small Kindnesses
chapters.summary: Kestrel's POV. Kestrel interviews witnesses from the original trial and finds each one's account subtly reshaped over time — all in directions that favor Brand's narrative. Memory as a communal project. Beat: creeping dread beneath polite conversation.

chapters.title: What the Child Saw
chapters.summary: Kestrel's POV, interleaved flashback. Eleven-year-old Kestrel gave testimony placing Okafor near the scene; the full memory returns: they were coached, gently, by a kind officer with a familiar voice. Beat: shame surfacing after years underwater.

chapters.title: A Threat, Politely Delivered
chapters.summary: Kestrel's POV. An anonymous note warns Kestrel off, quoting their own childhood statement back at them word for word — something only the trial transcript or a participant would know. Beat: the watcher becomes the watched.

chapters.title: The Bench by the Water
chapters.summary: Okafor's POV. Hidden and terrified, Okafor explains why he never fled: running would confirm guilt, and he wants his name cleared, not just his life. He remembers Kestrel from the courtroom — a child who wouldn't meet his eyes. Beat: dignity under erasure.

chapters.title: Ledgers and Lies
chapters.summary: Kestrel's POV. Insurance records show Brand took out policies on evidence storage and property tied to the case; financial threads suggest he profited from the conviction through a land deal. Circumstantial, but converging. Beat: the puzzle clicking, too slowly.

chapters.title: An Ally With Bad Timing
chapters.summary: Ada's POV. Ada and Kestrel formally partner, but Ada's impulsive public questions spook the town; a brick comes through her window. Kestrel realizes protecting Okafor means protecting Ada from herself. Beat: alliance forged under pressure.

chapters.title: The Voice on the Porch
chapters.summary: Kestrel's POV. The recovered memory finally resolves: the coaching officer's voice belongs to Brand himself, who was first on scene and alone with young Kestrel for forty minutes. Beat: certainty arriving like a cold current.

chapters.title: Everyone Swore It Was Closed
chapters.summary: Kestrel's POV. Kestrel confronts the town solicitor who handled the original trial; he admits doubts were buried because Marrow Bay needed the case closed — tourism, reputation, peace. Complicity wore a civic face. Beat: anger at systems, not just men.

chapters.title: Tail Lights in the Rain
chapters.summary: Okafor's POV. Okafor's safehouse is found; he escapes an attempted break-in but is injured, and the police — Brand's protégés — take his report with visible skepticism. Beat: no refuge left in official channels.

chapters.title: The Retrial Clock
chapters.summary: Kestrel's POV. The court denies a delay; Okafor must testify in nine days, which is exactly when any attempt on his life will come. Kestrel maps every route between safehouse and courthouse. Beat: countdown tension.

chapters.title: Confession, Draft One
chapters.summary: Ada's POV. Ada confronts Brand directly and records nothing useful — he's charming, unhurried, and mentions Kestrel's childhood by name. He knows exactly who is digging. Beat: the hunter admired by his prey.

chapters.title: What I Buried
chapters.summary: Kestrel's POV. Kestrel writes out their full reconstructed memory and their coached testimony, deciding to recant publicly even though perjury-adjacent exposure could end their career and standing. Beat: sacrifice chosen freely.

chapters.title: The Night Before
chapters.summary: Kestrel's POV. Stakeout of the courthouse route goes wrong; Kestrel intercepts Brand's fixer mid-attempt and is wounded, but photographs the payment handoff — Brand's signature habit, caught on camera. Beat: cost paid in blood.

chapters.title: The Quiet Confession
chapters.summary: Climax. Kestrel's POV. In the courthouse corridor, Kestrel corners Brand with the photos and their recanted testimony, forcing him to speak plainly where three witnesses and a recorder can hear — his vanity, not violence, betrays him. Beat: justice seized outside procedure.

chapters.title: Testimony
chapters.summary: Okafor's POV. Okafor testifies as Brand is arrested; the courtroom that once condemned him now hears the truth, including Kestrel's recantation read aloud. Beat: vindication that costs everyone something.

chapters.title: After the Verdict
chapters.summary: Ada's POV. The town reels; some thank Kestrel, others shun them. Ada and Okafor begin the slow work of rebuilding a name, and Ada asks Kestrel to stay in Marrow Bay. Beat: belonging redefined, not restored.

chapters.title: Open Case, Closed Book
chapters.summary: Kestrel's POV. Kestrel files their final report, keeps the memorial bench photo as a reminder that towns remember what they need to, and accepts Ada's invitation — choosing visibility over invisibility for the first time. Beat: quiet, earned hope.
